FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Nationally, flash floods kill more people than any other weather event and nearly half of those deaths are vehicle related, so when hazardous driving conditions are forecast the best choice is to stay home and avoid unnecessary travel [A01].
Why it matters: Handbook statistic on flood deaths, stated as the handbook states it.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
If a storm catches you on the road, slow down, switch cruise control off, stay alert, leave a gap of more than four seconds to the vehicle ahead, and take extra care at night or on roads you do not know [A01].
Why it matters: Cruise control off is a repeated storm rule.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
Flood waters may wash away or undermine bridges, culverts and roadbeds, so never drive around traffic barricades or past road closed signs, and obey every detour sign [A01].
Why it matters: Barricades and closures are absolute.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
Do not drive where water covers the road, because its depth is not obvious, it can hide washouts, and a vehicle's motor will stall in water, leaving you stranded or trapped [A01].
Why it matters: Water over the road is a no go.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
A vehicle that stalls in flood water should be abandoned at once, because rising water can carry off a car with everyone inside, many people have died trying to move a stalled vehicle, and even four inches of moving water can knock a walker down and hide hazards [A01].
Why it matters: Four inches of water is the walking threshold.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
Wind endangers all motorists but especially large vehicles and drivers towing trailers, so slower speeds are the best practice, and strong wind, heavy snow or ice can drop trees and wires into the road, which you must never approach or cross [A01].
Why it matters: Downed wires are never crossed.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A01
Check Weather Service flash flood and weather warnings and all hazardous driving notices before traveling [A01].
Why it matters: Pre trip warnings check.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A01
In fog, heavy rain or heavy snow use low beam headlights, and the law requires headlights on whenever you cannot clearly see persons or vehicles five hundred feet ahead [A01].
Why it matters: Five hundred feet is the headlight visibility trigger.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A01
Winter is the hardest driving season because of snow, ice and fewer daylight hours, so brakes, wipers, defroster, heater and exhaust must be in top condition, antifreeze checked, and the washer reservoir filled with a winter fluid [A01].
Why it matters: The winter vehicle checklist.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A01
Put good snow tires on all four wheels early so the first snowfall does not catch you without them, and never combine different types of tires on the same vehicle [A01].
Why it matters: All four wheels, same tire type.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A02
Many states allow metal studded tires only in winter conditions, and tires must always be properly inflated [A02].
Why it matters: Studs are seasonal; inflation is constant.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A02
During ice or snow storms, especially under a traveler's advisory, do not drive unless absolutely necessary, and if you must, clear all ice and snow from the entire vehicle, keep the wipers free of ice and the inside of the windows free of moisture [A02].
Why it matters: Whole vehicle clearing is required.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
When sleet, freezing rain or snow begins, black ice can form quickly and invisibly, bridges, ramps and overpasses freeze first, and slippery spots can remain after plows clear the highway [A02].
Why it matters: Bridges, ramps and overpasses freeze first.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
On winter roads allow extra travel time, increase following distance to more than four seconds, and remember that even four wheel or all wheel drive vehicles lack good traction on ice and every vehicle struggles to stop, curve and change lanes [A02].
Why it matters: Four wheel drive does not fix ice.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A02
Be especially careful near snowplows, which are hard to see in the snow cloud they create, are wider than other vehicles and often move slowly, and in winter travel by day, not alone, on main roads, with others informed of your route and schedule [A02].
Why it matters: Snowplow and trip planning rules.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A02
A winter vehicle kit should hold a windshield scraper and brush, a small shovel, kitty litter or sand, extra clothing, food and water, a cell phone, extra washer fluid, a basic first aid kit and a flashlight, and the gas tank should always be at least half full [A02].
Why it matters: Half a tank minimum in winter.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A02
If caught in a blizzard or stranded, pull off the highway, turn on the hazard lights, hang a distress flag from a door handle, antenna or window, and stay in the vehicle where rescuers are most likely to find you unless a sheltering building is clearly close, remembering that blowing snow distorts distance [A02].
Why it matters: Stay with the vehicle.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A02
While stranded run the engine and heater about ten minutes each hour, open a downwind window slightly for ventilation while the engine runs, and keep snow clear of the exhaust pipe to guard against carbon monoxide poisoning [A02].
Why it matters: Ten minutes per hour and a clear exhaust.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A02
While stranded exercise lightly to keep warm, insulate with maps, seat covers and floor mats, huddle with passengers and use a coat as a blanket, take turns sleeping so someone is always watching for rescuers, and drink fluids but never alcohol [A02].
Why it matters: No alcohol while stranded.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A02
While stranded conserve battery power by balancing lights, heat and radio against supply, turn on the inside light at night so crews can see you, and in a remote area stomp large letters spelling HELP or SOS in open snow and line them with rocks or limbs for searchers in aircraft [A02].
Why it matters: Battery balance and ground signals.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A03
Most skids come from a driver failing to adjust speed in time to road and traffic conditions such as snow, ice, rain, dirt, gravel and wet leaves, and cruise control must not be used in those conditions [A03].
Why it matters: Skids are a speed judgment failure.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A03
A rear wheel drive vehicle usually gives a feel of lost traction before a skid, but a front wheel drive may give no warning, and although front wheel drive handles better in snow its traction is not flawless, so its better feel must not tempt you to drive faster [A03].
Why it matters: Front wheel drive hides the warning.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A03
On a possibly slippery road drive slower, avoid sudden changes of speed or direction, slow by lifting off the gas, and if more slowing is needed squeeze the brakes with slow steady pressure, keep the wheels rolling, ease off if they begin to lock, and consider shifting to a lower gear [A03].
Why it matters: Squeeze, do not stab, the brakes.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A03
With anti-lock brakes use steady brake pressure and do not pump the brakes, following the owner's manual [A03].
Why it matters: No pumping with anti-lock brakes.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A03
Skid recovery is the same for front and rear wheel drive: do not hit the brakes, which worsens the skid, steer in the direction you want the vehicle to go, and expect to steer left and right a few times before full control returns [A03].
Why it matters: Steer where you want to go, no brakes.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A03
Stability control and similar improvements can help but never substitute for driver caution, four wheel and all wheel drive have better traction in snow but not on ice, and every driver should learn how the vehicle handles on ice or snow in an empty parking lot [A03].
Why it matters: Technology is not a substitute for caution.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A03
Anti-lock brakes let you brake and steer at the same time, and noise and vibration in the pedal are normal when they engage [A03].
Why it matters: Pedal pulsing is expected, not a fault.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A04
Pumping the brake or lifting your foot off the pedal disengages the anti-lock system, the owner's manual tells you whether the vehicle has it, and the anti-lock warning light shows briefly at start up [A04].
Why it matters: Keep the foot down.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A04
If the anti-lock warning light stays on after you begin driving, the anti-lock system is not working, although the vehicle still has ordinary brakes [A04].
Why it matters: A lit light means no anti-lock, not no brakes.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A04
Studies show that driving with low beam headlights on in daytime reduces the risk of head on collisions by more than twenty percent, and daytime running lights that come on automatically must not be mistaken for headlights [A04].
Why it matters: Handbook statistic on daytime low beams, stated as the handbook states it.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A04
When snow, rain or fog limit visibility you must turn the headlights on, the best practice is to drive with at least low beams on even by day, and parking lights are only for a parked vehicle [A04].
Why it matters: Parking lights are never driving lights.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A04
Night driving is more dangerous because you cannot see as far ahead, and the law requires headlights on from a half hour after sunset until a half hour before sunrise, so switch them on yourself because daytime running lights can make you think they already are [A04].
Why it matters: Half hour after sunset to half hour before sunrise.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A04
You always need to see four seconds ahead, and at night at forty miles per hour on low beams you are overdriving your headlights, unable to stop within the distance you can see [A04].
Why it matters: Forty on low beams outruns the light.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A04
Use high beams in open country with few other vehicles, keeping speed lower than by day even with them, and use low beams when approaching other vehicles or pedestrians, in areas with streetlights or fog, and when following another vehicle [A04].
Why it matters: Four low beam situations.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A04
A courteous night driver promptly dims the headlights when meeting or following another vehicle, and to avoid being blinded by oncoming lights looks ahead toward the right edge of the road rather than directly at them [A04].
Why it matters: Look right to beat glare.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0050]

Misconceptions:
- Pumping the brakes helps in every emergency stop: false, pumping disengages anti-lock brakes; hold steady pressure and let the pedal pulse.
- Braking is the first step in a skid: false, braking makes a skid worse; steer where you want to go.
- Four wheel drive stops and corners well on ice: false, it helps in snow but not on ice, and every vehicle struggles to stop and turn on winter roads.
- Daytime running lights satisfy the night headlight law: false, you must switch on the headlights yourself from a half hour after sunset.
- Shallow moving water is safe to walk or drive through: false, four inches can knock a walker down and a motor stalls in water; stay out and abandon a stalled car.

Mnemonics:
- Ten minutes an hour, window cracked, exhaust clear: the stranded engine routine.
- Steady, not pumped: anti-lock braking in two words.
- Half hour after, half hour before: the headlight clock around sunset and sunrise.
- Five hundred feet or lights on: the visibility headlight rule.

Glossary:
- Black ice: a thin, nearly invisible ice layer that forms quickly when sleet, freezing rain or snow begin, first on bridges, ramps and overpasses
- Anti-lock brakes: a braking system that lets you brake and steer at once, used with steady pressure and signaled by a pulsing pedal
- Overdriving your headlights: driving so fast at night that you cannot stop within the distance your headlights show
- Daytime running lights: automatic low intensity lights for daytime visibility that are not a substitute for headlights
- Traveler's advisory: a weather warning during which driving should be avoided unless absolutely necessary
